title: An Uber Eats Driver Ran Over a Man Twice on a Birmingham Pavement. He Was Driving While Disqualified.
excerpt: Harinderpal Athwal was jailed for more than 11 years after killing a father walking hand-in-hand with his wife. The case has reignited questions about gig platforms and driver vetting in the UK.
body:
On December 16, just days before Christmas, a couple walked hand-in-hand along Soho Road in Birmingham — one of the city's busiest streets and the heart of its South Asian community. What happened next was captured in CCTV footage that prosecutors described as deeply disturbing.

Harinderpal Athwal, a 41-year-old Uber Eats driver from Tividale in the West Midlands, was at the wheel of a Vauxhall Corsa when he suddenly swerved into oncoming traffic, mounted the pavement, and struck the couple without slowing down. The 54-year-old husband was hit with devastating force. But the horror did not end there: footage showed Athwal reversing his car away from the injured man, then driving forward again — striking the victim a second time before fleeing the scene.

The man died at the scene. His 47-year-old wife was rushed to hospital with injuries that would permanently alter her life.

'He Was My Emotional Support'

In a victim impact statement read before Birmingham Crown Court, the widow described a grief so total that it had consumed every aspect of her existence.

"I cry every day for my husband. He was my emotional support and my strength," she told the court. "He managed our finances, made important decisions and kept our family stable. Without him, I feel completely lost."

She directed particular anger at Athwal's decision to flee. "Athwal's actions in driving away and refusing to help showed complete disregard for what he had done," she said. "No sentence will ever bring back the family's loved one, but we hope this brings them some peace."

A Catalogue of Violations

When police arrested Athwal less than 24 hours after the crash, they discovered something that transformed the case from a tragic accident into something far more damning: Athwal had been disqualified from driving. He held no valid licence. He carried no insurance. He had no legal right to be behind the wheel of any vehicle, let alone one operating under the banner of a commercial delivery platform.

Athwal pleaded guilty to six charges: causing death by dangerous driving, causing serious injury by dangerous driving, driving while disqualified, driving without a licence and insurance, failing to stop after an accident, and failing to report the crash. At Birmingham Crown Court, he was sentenced to 11 years and three months in prison and banned from driving for 20 years.

Detective Sergeant Julie Lyman of West Midlands Police described his behaviour as "cruel and heartless."

The Gig Economy's Blind Spot

The case has reignited scrutiny of how ride-hailing and delivery platforms vet the drivers they deploy onto British roads. Uber Eats, like other gig-economy platforms, requires drivers to hold valid licences and permits. But enforcement of those requirements has long been criticised as inconsistent, particularly for food delivery services that operate with less regulatory oversight than passenger ride-hailing.

In Birmingham — home to one of the UK's largest South Asian populations — the case has resonated with particular force. Soho Road is not merely a commercial thoroughfare; it is the cultural spine of the city's Punjabi, Pakistani, and Bangladeshi communities. That the victim was killed there, by a driver operating under the umbrella of a globally recognised platform, has deepened community anger.

Uber said in a statement that safety is a priority and that it works with law enforcement. The company did not comment on how Athwal was able to operate on its platform while disqualified from driving.

What the Diaspora Sees

For British Indians, the case touches on several anxieties that run deeper than a single criminal act. The gig economy employs a disproportionate number of South Asian workers in the UK, many of whom drive for platforms like Uber Eats, Deliveroo, and Just Eat. These workers often operate under enormous financial pressure, with minimal protections and incentive structures that reward speed over safety.

The question now being asked in community forums and on social media is straightforward: if a disqualified driver can operate freely on a major delivery platform, what other safeguards are being quietly bypassed?

Athwal will serve at least two-thirds of his sentence before becoming eligible for release. The victim's widow and children continue to rebuild a life that was shattered on a pavement where they should have been safe.
